Threat.value: I constantly scan my surroundings for signs of danger
I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home

Memory.value: Some moments of the event are extremely clear while others are completely blank
I feel like I am only remembering parts of what happened and the rest is missing
When the memory returns I feel physical pain in the same parts of my body as during the event

vignette:
Rasha is a 38-year-old housekeeper who came to therapy at her husband’s urging, though she admitted she was tired of living in a state of constant vigilance. Eight months ago, she was cleaning a hotel room when a male guest, who had been drinking, returned unexpectedly and locked the door behind him. He shouted at her for being in his room, grabbed her by the shoulders, and shoved her against the wall before forcing her to kneel and scrub the floor while he stood over her, yelling. The assault lasted only a few minutes before he left, but in those moments Rasha’s mind fractured. She remembers the pressure of his hands on her collarbones with excruciating clarity—she can still feel a dull ache in her shoulders when the memory surfaces—but she cannot recall how she got out of the room or who found her afterward. There are stretches of blankness that feel like missing teeth in her memory: the sound of the door opening, the face of the first person who helped her, the walk to the manager’s office. She has tried to piece it together, but the gaps remain, and they frighten her more than the parts she remembers.

In the weeks after the assault, Rasha began to notice changes in how she moved through the world. At work, she now refuses to clean any room unless the door is propped open with a heavy cart, and she listens constantly for footsteps, for keys in locks, for the particular pitch of a man’s voice in the hallway. She has asked her supervisor to assign her only to rooms on the ground floor, where she can see the exit, and she has begun skipping rooms that require her to be alone for more than a few minutes. Her manager has grown frustrated, and Rasha knows she is risking her job, but the thought of being trapped again is worse than any consequence. At home, she checks every window and door before she can sit down, and she has developed a habit of pausing mid-conversation to listen for sounds she cannot name—a creak in the hallway, the click of a lock. Her husband has noticed that she startles when he clears his throat, and she has stopped letting him come up behind her without warning. She knows he is trying to be patient, but she can feel his worry hardening into resentment.

What frightens Rasha most is not the memory itself but the certainty that another assault is waiting for her. She scans every room she enters for exits, for objects that could be used as weapons, for the faces of men who look like they might shout. She has come to believe that she was targeted because she was alone and small, and that if she is not constantly watching, she will be caught again. This scanning has made it nearly impossible to concentrate—she cannot follow a television show, she loses the thread of her own thoughts, and she has stopped reading because the words float away before she can grasp them. At night, she lies awake listening for the sound of someone entering the apartment, even though her husband is beside her and the door is locked twice.

She came to therapy because she caught herself rehearsing what she would do if a man shouted at her in the grocery store—where she would run, how she would scream—and she realized she had been doing this for hours every day without noticing. She is hoping, she said quietly, to feel like her body belongs to her again, though she is not sure that is possible. She is most afraid that the gaps in her memory will never fill in, and that she will spend the rest of her life waiting for the next time someone forces her to her knees.
